title: Conversion across streams
hookLine: requirements differ, and not every stream recognizes every conversion

lines: THY PEOPLE SHALL BE MY PEOPLE.
cards: "Thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God." A young widow from Moab says it on a road, to her mother-in-law, who has just told her, again, to go home. Ruth does not go home.

She walks into a people not her own, and the book that bears her name ends with a family tree: her great-grandson is King David. Tradition remembers her as someone who joined the Jewish people by choice.
You met another, Ovadiah, on day forty-five. How that choosing works today is today's word.

teach.b: Conversion across streams. The old shape first. The Talmud describes someone who comes to convert.

They are asked why, and told honestly that the Jewish people has known hardship. If they still say, I know, and I want this, they are taught some of the commandments, light ones and weighty ones, and welcomed.
In Orthodox and Conservative Judaism, conversion usually means a time of study, a court of three called a beit din, immersion in a mikveh, a ritual bath, and for men, circumcision.
Reform and Reconstructionist rabbis also ask for study and commitment; how they handle immersion and circumcision varies from community to community. Then the hard part.

teach.h: NOT EVERY STREAM RECOGNIZES EVERY CONVERSION.
teach.b: Because the streams disagree about authority, not every stream recognizes every other stream's conversions. Orthodox courts, for instance, accept conversions done to Orthodox standards.

A person can stand inside one community as a Jew and be asked questions in another. That is painful, and each stream would say it is guarding something it holds sacred, not shutting anyone out lightly. And the welcome.
The Torah commands that the stranger who lives among you "shall be unto you as one born among you, and thou shalt love him as thyself."
The Talmud adds that you must never remind a convert of who they used to be. Once someone has come in, they are simply family. Requirements differ across the streams.
The Torah's welcome stands in the scripture they share.

how: People who convert to Judaism study with a rabbi and join a community; depending on the stream, conversion includes a beit din, immersion in a mikveh and, for men, circumcision, and the convert takes a Hebrew name.

o: a ceremony where a Jewish couple renews its vows
switching from one Jewish movement to another one
joining the Jewish people by choice, in each stream's way

games.q: you're a rabbi in the Talmud's story, and someone asks to convert. what do you do first?
o: welcome them at once and ask nothing.
ask why, and tell them honestly about hardship.
games.why: they are asked why and told the truth; if they still say I know, and I want this, they are taught and welcomed.

practice: Bring to mind someone who joined something by choice: a person who converted, a new citizen, someone who married into a family and learned its jokes, a newcomer at work. Remember a moment when they might have felt like an outsider.
Then picture a small welcome you could give them: their name said warmly, a seat saved, a question about their story asked with real interest, never a reminder of where they came from.

wordCard.voice: Conversion across streams. Joining the Jewish people by choice: requirements differ from stream to stream, and not every stream recognizes every conversion. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: the stranger who lives among you, and in rabbinic Hebrew, a convert.

carryVoice: Your line: many doors. Different requirements across the streams, and the same old welcome. Until tomorrow.
